title: What Are Backlinks? How to Get Them Safely | KivoReach
description: Backlinks explained: what they are, why they matter for SEO, which links Google treats as spam, and safe ways to get backlinks for a small website.

article.summary: Backlinks are links from other websites to yours. They help search engines find and judge your pages, but buying them breaks Google's rules. Here is how to earn them.
takeaways: A backlink is a link from another website to yours.
Links help search engines discover pages and can signal that content is worth reading.
Buying links, excessive link swaps and automated link building are link spam under Google's policies; earn links with useful pages instead.
article.author: KivoReach

blocks.text: What are backlinks? How to get them safely

blocks.html: A backlink is a link on another website that points to yours. If a local news site links to your shop's page, that is a backlink for you. Backlinks are the best-known part of off-page SEO, and also the part where most people get bad advice.

Search engines discover new pages by following links, so a link from a known site helps your page get found. Google's guide to how Search works describes links as one of the ways it finds pages. Links are also a sign of attention: people link to things they find useful. That is why a few links from relevant, trusted sites are worth more than many from unrelated or low-quality ones.

blocks.caption: Links help pages get discovered and show that others value them.
How Google's policies separate earned links from link spam
rows: A site links to your page because it is useful

A local paper writes about your business
Excessive link exchanges ("link to me and I'll link to you")
A partner lists you, with the link marked as sponsored if paid
Automated programs or services that create links to your site
You are listed in a genuine, relevant directory
Low-quality directory or bookmark site links
Your guest article helps readers, with links marked appropriately
Keyword-stuffed links in articles, guest posts or press releases spread across many sites

blocks.html: Google's spam policies define link spam as creating links mainly to manipulate rankings. If a link is paid for or sponsored, it should carry rel="sponsored" (or nofollow) so it passes no ranking credit.

items.title: Publish something worth linking to
items.html: A clear guide, a free tool, local data you collected, or a page that answers a common question better than anyone else.

items.title: Tell the people who care
items.html: Share it with communities, partners and customers who would find it useful, without asking for a link in return.

items.title: Get listed where customers look
items.html: Your Google Business Profile, your industry's genuine directories and local business associations.

items.title: Work with real partners
items.html: Suppliers, clients and event organisers often list the businesses they work with.

items.title: Fix broken links to you
items.html: If someone links to a page of yours that moved, ask them to update it, or redirect the old address to the new one.

blocks.html: Use our free Broken Link Checker to make sure the links on your own pages work, and Website Comparison to compare your site with a competitor's.

Scores such as Domain Authority or Domain Rating are made by private SEO companies to estimate a site's link strength. They are not Google measures. They can be handy for comparing sites, but improving a third-party score is not the goal; earning real links from relevant sites is.

items: You have at least one page that is genuinely useful to link to
Your Business Profile and real directory listings are complete
Paid or sponsored links are marked rel="sponsored" or nofollow
No link packages, link swaps or automated link building
Old addresses that others link to redirect to the right page

blocks.question: How many backlinks do I need?
blocks.answer: There is no number. Google does not publish one, and a few relevant links from trusted sites can matter more than many weak ones. Focus on earning links to your most useful pages.

blocks.question: Can link schemes hurt my site?
blocks.answer: Yes. Google's spam policies say it detects violations with automated systems and, when needed, human review, and that sites breaking the policies may rank lower or not appear at all. Do not buy links or join link networks.

blocks.question: Are nofollow links useless?
blocks.answer: No. They can still bring visitors and attention. Google's guidance is to mark paid or sponsored links with rel="sponsored" (nofollow is still accepted) so that they pass no ranking credit.
